The decision worth defending is what a check may look at. Every number comes from the robot's own motion on

except a wall-clock guard, because a dead simulation also stops simulated time, and a simulated deadline would then never arrive.

What we can now show: five runs in a row pass, with the margin between each measured number and its limit written down. And the runner fails two different ways on purpose: cutting the relay fails exactly the distance check, and killing Gazebo mid-run lets the guard end it on the time check instead of hanging forever.

Everything after this topic is a scenario: normal operation, odometry that stops, a cancelled mission. Each of them starts the world headless, does something to the robot, and has to answer one question without a person watching. Four decisions settle how that answer is produced, and each costs something to change later.
The verdict comes from the robot's own motion, measured by the simulator and published on
, and never from the commands the nodes sent. The architecture topic gave the reason: a stop that was published is not proof that the robot stopped.
is the bridge's topic, upstream of the relay, so a scenario that cuts the relay still sees what the robot did.
The timetable is in simulated time. A busy machine changes how long a run takes on your watch, and it must not change what the robot did. Simulated time comes from
and every deadline it keeps is a simulated deadline. One deadline is different and stays on the wall clock, which is Build 2's subject.
The numbers a scenario requires are logic, so they live in
where a test reaches them without ROS, next to the supervisor's rules. The node measures and hands them over; it decides nothing.

A sample's time is the odometry message's stamp, the moment the pose was true. That is the opposite of the supervisor's choice, and for a reason worth saying out loud: freshness is a question about delivery, so it uses the arrival time, and a measurement is a question about the thing measured, so it uses the stamp.
The scenario this topic runs is called

, and its job is to prove the runner rather than the robot. It warms up for 2 s, drives forward at 0.2 m/s for 3 s, and then stops commanding and gives the robot 3 s to come to rest. Its four requirements each carry their arithmetic:

items.v: the run lasted at least the 8 s of its plan, which fails when the clock stopped or the guard ended the run early;
the robot moved at least 0.30 m, about half of the 3 s × 0.2 m/s = 0.60 m the drive phase asks for, so a slow start passes and a robot that never moved fails;
its top speed stayed at or below 0.30 m/s, which catches a runaway robot and a command in the wrong unit;

it came to rest at most 1.50 s after the last command. The supervisor's own arithmetic predicts 0.75 s: 0.50 to 0.55 s until the first stop goes out, 0.2 s of braking at 1 m/s², and up to one odometry period of 33 ms before
shows it. The limit is twice that, so a busy machine doesn't turn a pass into a failure.

By the end of this session,
is the one command: it starts the world headless, runs the scenario, shuts everything down and prints pass or fail.

Two pieces make that one command. A launch file starts the bench, the relay and the runner, and ends the whole group when the runner exits; a script at the top of the repository runs the launch file, reads the verdict and turns it into an exit code. The verdict is a file rather than the launch command's exit code on purpose: a launch file runs several processes, and one number at the end can't say which of them decided the scenario, or whether it decided anything at all.

blocks.text:
"""Runs one Test Bench scenario headless: the bench, the relay and the scenario runner."""
import os

from ament_index_python.packages import get_package_share_directory
from launch import LaunchDescription
from launch.actions import DeclareLaunchArgument, IncludeLaunchDescription, RegisterEventHandler, Shutdown
from launch.conditions import IfCondition
from launch.event_handlers import OnProcessExit
from launch.launch_description_sources import PythonLaunchDescriptionSource
from launch.substitutions import LaunchConfiguration
from launch_ros.actions import Node


def generate_launch_description():
    bench = IncludeLaunchDescription(
        PythonLaunchDescriptionSource(
            os.path.join(get_package_share_directory('bench_sim'), 'launch', 'bench.launch.py')),
        launch_arguments={'headless': 'True'}.items())
    relay = Node(package='bench_nodes', executable='odom_relay', output='screen',
                 condition=IfCondition(LaunchConfiguration('relay')))
    runner = Node(package='bench_nodes', executable='scenario_runner', output='screen',
                  parameters=[{'use_sim_time': True,
                               'scenario': LaunchConfiguration('scenario'),
                               'verdict_file': LaunchConfiguration('verdict_file')}])
    return LaunchDescription([
        DeclareLaunchArgument('scenario', default_value='smoke'),
        DeclareLaunchArgument('verdict_file'),
        DeclareLaunchArgument('relay', default_value='True'),
        bench,
        relay,
        runner,
        RegisterEventHandler(OnProcessExit(target_action=runner, on_exit=[Shutdown(reason='the scenario ended')])),
    ])

c.v: from the supervisor topic rather than repeating the world and the supervisor, and it brings the relay into a launch file for the first time; until now the relay ran in a terminal of its own so that Ctrl+C could stop it alone.
is declared without a default, so a run that forgets it stops with an error instead of throwing its result away. The event handler is what makes the group end: when the runner's process exits,
sends every other process a signal, and Gazebo, the bridge,
, the supervisor and the relay stop with it. The relay has a condition, which Build 4 uses to run the same scenario with the odometry path broken.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# run_scenario.sh NAME [launch arguments]: runs scenario NAME headless and prints its verdict.
# Exit code 0 means it passed.
cd "$(dirname "$0")"
source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
source install/setup.bash
set -euo pipefail
name=${1:?usage: ./run_scenario.sh NAME [launch arguments]}
mkdir -p results
verdict="$PWD/results/$name.txt"
rm -f "$verdict"
{ git rev-parse HEAD
  lsb_release -ds
  gz sim --version
  dpkg-query -W ros-jazzy-nav2-minimal-tb3-sim; } > "results/$name.env"
timeout --signal=INT 180 ros2 launch bench_sim scenario.launch.py \
  scenario:="$name" verdict_file:="$verdict" "${@:2}" || true
test -s "$verdict" || { echo "fail: the runner wrote no verdict"; exit 1; }
cat "$verdict"
head -1 "$verdict" | grep -qx pass

c.v: The measured numbers differ between runs, and the verdict must not. Write down the smallest and the largest of each. Then compare each number with its limit: the margin you have is what tells you whether the limit is a real requirement or a coin toss. A distance that lands within a centimetre of 0.30 m means the limit is wrong for this scenario, not that the robot is unreliable.

items.v: Measure two numbers, and keep them apart. The first is what one run costs, which decides whether scenarios can run on every push:

c.v: Most of that wall time is Gazebo starting, the packages loading and discovery finishing, and the scenario's 8 s of simulated time is the smaller part of it. So don't divide one by the other. The second number, how fast the simulation itself runs, comes from the scenario's own stretch: the runner logs

and then the verdict, so the wall clock between those two lines covers the 8 s of the plan and nothing else. Divide the 8 s by that. Gazebo computes the same thing for itself and publishes it on its statistics topic, which is the cross-check:

blocks.text: gz topic -e -t /stats      # while a scenario runs; read real_time_factor, then Ctrl+C

c.v: Write both numbers down with the machine they came from. Headless and without rendering, the sandbox world is a small one; measure yours rather than trusting a number from another machine.

items.v: Write down what makes two runs differ and what is pinned. Differing: the wall time Gazebo needs to start, the order in which the nodes discover each other, how many samples arrive before the warm-up ends, and the machine's load. Pinned: the world file and the robot's spawn pose from
, the version of that package, the supervisor's two timeouts, the runner's plan and drive speed, and the commit, all of which the

file and the parameters already record. Physics adds its own: Gazebo steps the world at a fixed step size, so the robot's motion is repeatable for the same sequence of commands, and the commands arrive at slightly different simulated moments each run.
